c.v: When someone dies in Sterling Heights because another person or company was careless, Michigan’s Wrongful Death Act (MCL 600.2922) gives the family a claim, but not in the way many families expect. The claim belongs to the estate, not to the spouse or children directly. It must be brought by a personal representative appointed by the probate court. The recovery is divided among family members by a judge. And the deadline depends on what caused the death: a crash at Van Dyke and 18½ Mile, a truck at a plant gate, a driver leaving a Hall Road bar, a death on the job, a hospital error, a nursing home. Some of those deadlines are 120 days. This page explains how the process works for a Sterling Heights family and what to do in the first weeks.

sections.heading: How a Sterling Heights wrongful death claim works

c.v: Only the personal representative can bring the claim (MCL 600.2922(2)). Where the person lived in Sterling Heights, the estate is opened in the Macomb County Probate Court at 40 N. Main Street in Mount Clemens. If there is a will naming a personal representative, that person petitions for appointment; if not, a family member, usually the spouse or an adult child, petitions under Michigan’s priority rules (MCL 700.3203). The court issues letters of authority, and the personal representative then has standing to hire a lawyer for the estate and file. We file the petition as the first legal step.

Within 30 days after filing suit, the personal representative must notify in writing every person who may share in the recovery: the spouse, children, descendants, parents, grandparents, brothers and sisters, the children of the deceased’s spouse, and anyone named in the will (MCL 600.2922(2)–(4)). The Act does not rank them in a fixed order of priority; the court divides the recovery according to each person’s loss.

The suit is the injury claim the person would have had, brought by the estate against whoever caused the death. Death claims are filed in circuit court, not the 41A District Court on Dodge Park Road, which hears civil cases only up to $25,000. For a death in Sterling Heights that is usually the Sixteenth Judicial Circuit Court in Mount Clemens. Where the crash was on Dequindre, or a defendant is in Oakland County, the Oakland County Circuit Court may also be a proper venue (MCL 600.1629). Claims against the State go to the Court of Claims.

If the person who died was partly at fault, the damages are reduced by that share. If their fault was greater than the combined fault of everyone else, the estate cannot recover noneconomic damages, but can still recover reduced economic damages (MCL 600.2959). In an auto case, the no-fault act bars noneconomic damages at more than 50 percent fault (MCL 500.3135(2)(b)).

After a settlement or verdict, the personal representative proposes a division among the eligible family members, with notice to each. If they agree, the court approves it; if not, the court decides based on each person’s relationship and loss (MCL 600.2922(6)). Fees and costs are approved at the same hearing. Because a judge divides the money, no family member should sign anything with an insurer; a release signed by one relative does not settle the estate’s claim.

faqs.question: Who can file a wrongful death lawsuit in Sterling Heights?

answer.v: Only the personal representative of the estate, appointed by the Macomb County Probate Court for a Sterling Heights resident. A spouse, child, or parent can be appointed, but must be appointed before the claim can be filed.

The spouse, children, descendants, parents, grandparents, siblings, the children of the deceased’s spouse, and anyone named in the will may share. The probate court divides the recovery according to each person’s loss after notice to each of them.

Three years from the death for crash, fall, and premises claims; two years with a 182-day notice for medical malpractice; two years for a dram shop claim; one year to claim no-fault survivor’s loss benefits; and 120 days to notify the City or the Department of Roads of a road defect.

faqs.question: My husband died at the plant. Can we sue?

answer.v: Usually not the employer, which owes workers’ compensation death benefits instead, unless the narrow intentional tort exception applies. But a contractor, a property owner, or the maker of a defective machine whose negligence caused the death can be sued, and that suit is the wrongful death claim.
Michigan does not award punitive damages in wrongful death cases. The family recovers the losses the Act lists, including loss of companionship, which has no cap outside medical malpractice.

faqs.question: Is there a lawsuit if the driver was charged with a crime?

answer.v: Yes. The criminal case and the family’s claim are separate. The family does not have to wait for the criminal case, and the civil deadlines keep running.
